questions.prompt: A director realizes, halfway through a discussion, that the contract under consideration involves her brother-in-law’s company. What should she do?

options.text: Stay quiet and abstain from the vote
Declare the interest right away, then leave for the rest of the discussion and the vote
Finish the discussion, then declare it before the vote
Nothing; in-laws don’t count as family

questions.explanation: Declare as soon as you become aware of the conflict, even mid-discussion, then abstain and leave. The declaration should be recorded in the minutes.

questions.prompt: The ED/CEO mentions that payroll remittances were late last month. Why should the board treat this seriously?

options.text: Because it may affect the strategic plan
It isn’t a board matter; payroll is a management responsibility
Because directors can be personally liable for unremitted source deductions
Because it must be reported in the T3010

questions.explanation: Directors can be personally liable for unremitted source deductions. The board should confirm remittances are current and ask what will prevent a repeat.

questions.prompt: A director disagrees strongly with a board decision. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Ask for the dissent to be recorded in the minutes and support the decision publicly
Explain the disagreement on social media so the community knows
Tell staff privately that the decision was a mistake
Refuse to implement the decision

questions.explanation: The board speaks with one voice. A director can have dissent recorded, raise it again through proper process later, or resign if they cannot support the decision in good conscience.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a governance decision rather than a management one?

options.text: Choosing the caterer for the volunteer appreciation event
Scheduling staff vacation
Selecting the office’s accounting software
Setting the organization’s risk tolerance and approving a reserves policy

questions.explanation: Setting risk tolerance and policy is board work. Day-to-day operational choices belong to management.

questions.prompt: A staff member receives an email, apparently from a long-time supplier, asking to change the bank account for future payments. What should the board want to know?

options.text: Whether the supplier offers a discount for the change
Whether there are controls requiring independent verification of payment-detail changes before money moves
Nothing; this is too operational for the board
Which staff member received the email, so they can be disciplined

questions.explanation: Payment-redirection fraud is common. The board’s role is to make sure controls exist, such as confirming changes by phone using a known number, not to handle the transaction itself.

questions.prompt: A director who sits on a funder’s board as well is asked to vote on a funding agreement with that funder. The best approach is to:

options.text: Vote, since both organizations want the agreement
Abstain from the vote but stay for the discussion
Declare the dual role, abstain and leave the room for the discussion and vote
Resign from one of the boards before the meeting

questions.explanation: Serving on both boards creates a conflict of duties. Declare, Abstain, Leave applies even when the interests appear aligned.
